steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that combines a vector-quantised image autoencoder with a discrete diffusion model for image generation. Explain the weaknesses of autoregressive priors and of standard diffusion models, then present our model and its contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- VQ-VAE and autoregressive priors; their limitations
- Diffusion models capture global information
- But diffusion is slow
- Our method: VQ-DDM
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- VQ-VAE (cite): compress images into discrete representations for generation
  - autoregressive model over discrete latent space: PixelCNN family (cite), transformers family (cite)
  - huge number of parameters
  - only see observed pixels (left upper part), inductive bias from strict scan order (cite)
  - conditional info at end of sequence hard to use
- Denoising Diffusion Model
  - mitigates lack of global information (cite)
  - comparable or SOTA in text (cite), image (cite), speech (cite)
  - parameterized Markov chains, simple -> sophisticated distributions, finite steps
  - starts from isotropic Gaussian, continuous state space; reverses process that adds Gaussian noise
  - each reverse step uses global information of previous step
- Slow
  - huge time and computation to generate images; reverse process has thousands of steps
  - training need not iterate all steps, sampling does; slower than GANs, even autoregressive
  - fewer sampling steps (cite), but each step still full-resolution image
- VQ-DDM (Vector Quantized Discrete Diffusion Model)
  - discrete VAE + discrete diffusion model
  - two stages: (1) discrete representation of images, (2) fit prior over latent codes with discrete diffusion
  - discrete scheme -> less compute and time for high-resolution images
  - solves lack of global content and too many parameters of autoregressive models
  - codebook bias limits quality; size depends on categories -> re-build and fine-tune (ReFiT), higher utilization, fewer parameters
- Contributions
  - discrete diffusion prior over latent codes; global information, avoids sequential bias
  - ReFiT: code usage of VQ-GAN 31.85\% -> 97.07\%; reconstruction FID 10.18 -> 5.64 on CelebA-HQ 256\times 256
  - efficient: 120M parameters (Figure 1); beats VQ-VAE-2 (~10B), comparable to VQ-GAN (1B); 10 \sim 100 times faster than other diffusion models (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Vector Quantised Variational AutoEncoder (VQ-VAE) is a popular method for compressing images into discrete representations for generation. Usually the image is compressed and discretized by a convolutional network, and then an autoregressive model is used to model and sample in the discrete latent space, for example the PixelCNN family or the transformers family. But these autoregressive models have a huge number of model parameters, and they can also only make predictions based on the observed pixels (the left upper part of the target pixel), because of the inductive bias that comes from strictly following the progressive scan order. If the conditional information is at the end of the autoregressive sequence, the model has difficulty getting the relevant information.

A recent alternative generative model is the Denoising Diffusion Model, which can mitigate the lack of global information. It also gets comparable or state-of-the-art performance in text, image and speech generation tasks. Diffusion models are parameterized Markov chains that are trained to translate simple distributions to more sophisticated target data distributions in a finite set of steps. Usually the Markov chain starts with an isotropic Gaussian distribution in continuous state space, and the transitions of the chain reverse a diffusion process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to source images. In the inverse process the current step is based on the global information of the previous step in the chain, and this is what gives the diffusion model the ability to capture global information.

However, the diffusion model has a big disadvantage, which is that generating images takes an enormous amount of time and computation. This is mainly because the reverse process usually has thousands of steps. During training we do not need to iterate through all the steps, but when generating a sample all the steps are still needed, so it is much slower than GANs and even autoregressive models.

Some recent works have tried to address this by decreasing the number of sampling steps, but the computation cost is still high, because each step of the reverse process generates a full-resolution image.

Our method: VQ-DDM (Vector Quantized Discrete Diffusion Model)
- discrete VAE + discrete diffusion model
- two stages: (1) discrete representation of images, (2) fit prior over latent codes with discrete diffusion
- discrete scheme -> less compute and time for high-resolution images
- fixes lack of global content and too many parameters of autoregressive models
- codebook bias -> re-build and fine-tune (ReFiT), higher utilization, fewer parameters

Contributions
- discrete diffusion prior over latent codes; global information, no sequential bias
- ReFiT: VQ-GAN code usage 31.85\% -> 97.07\%; reconstruction FID 10.18 -> 5.64 on CelebA-HQ 256\times 256
- 120M parameters (Figure 1); beats VQ-VAE-2 (~10B), comparable to VQ-GAN (1B); 10 \sim 100 times faster than other diffusion models

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Vector Quantised Variational AutoEncoder (VQ-VAE) is a popular method for compressing images into discrete representations for generation. Usually the image is compressed and discretized by a convolutional network, and then an autoregressive model is used to model and sample in the discrete latent space, for example the PixelCNN family or the transformers family. But these autoregressive models have a huge number of model parameters, and they can also only make predictions based on the observed pixels (the left upper part of the target pixel), because of the inductive bias that comes from strictly following the progressive scan order. If the conditional information is at the end of the autoregressive sequence, the model has difficulty getting the relevant information.

A recent alternative generative model is the Denoising Diffusion Model, which can mitigate the lack of global information. It also gets comparable or state-of-the-art performance in text, image and speech generation tasks. Diffusion models are parameterized Markov chains that are trained to translate simple distributions to more sophisticated target data distributions in a finite set of steps. Usually the Markov chain starts with an isotropic Gaussian distribution in continuous state space, and the transitions of the chain reverse a diffusion process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to source images. In the inverse process the current step is based on the global information of the previous step in the chain, and this is what gives the diffusion model the ability to capture global information.

However, the diffusion model has a big disadvantage, which is that generating images takes an enormous amount of time and computation. This is mainly because the reverse process usually has thousands of steps. During training we do not need to iterate through all the steps, but when generating a sample all the steps are still needed, so it is much slower than GANs and even autoregressive models.

Some recent works have tried to address this by decreasing the number of sampling steps, but the computation cost is still high, because each step of the reverse process generates a full-resolution image.

In this work we propose the Vector Quantized Discrete Diffusion Model (VQ-DDM), a versatile framework for image generation made of a discrete variational autoencoder and a discrete diffusion model. VQ-DDM has two stages: (1) learning an abundant and efficient discrete representation of images, and (2) fitting the prior distribution of these latent visual codes with the discrete diffusion model.

Because it uses a discrete scheme, VQ-DDM greatly reduces the computational resources and the time needed to generate high-resolution images. Fitting the latent variable prior with the discrete diffusion model also solves the common problem of autoregressive models, which is the lack of global content and the overly large number of parameters. Also, a bias of the codebook will limit generation quality, and the model size also depends on the number of categories, so we propose a re-build and fine-tune (ReFiT) strategy to build a codebook with higher utilization, which also reduces the number of parameters in our model.

In summary, our key contributions are:

- VQ-DDM fits the prior over discrete latent codes with a discrete diffusion model. Using the diffusion model lets the generative model consider global information instead of only the partially seen context, so sequential bias is avoided.

- We propose a ReFiT approach that improves the utilisation of latent representations in the visual codebook. It increases the code usage of VQ-GAN from 31.85\% to 97.07\%, and the FID between the reconstruction image and the original training image goes down from 10.18 to 5.64 on CelebA-HQ 256\times 256.

- VQ-DDM is very efficient in both number of parameters and generation speed. As Figure 1 shows, with only 120M parameters it outperforms VQ-VAE-2, which has around 10B parameters, and it is comparable with VQ-GAN with 1B parameters in image quality for image generation tasks. It is also 10 \sim 100 times faster than other diffusion models for image generation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Vector Quantised Variational AutoEncoder (VQ-VAE) [1] is a popular method developed to compress images into discrete representations for generation. Typically, after compression and discretization by a convolutional network, an autoregressive model is used to model and sample in the discrete latent space, including the PixelCNN family [2,3,4], the transformers family [5,6], etc. However, besides the disadvantage of a huge number of model parameters, these autoregressive models can only make predictions based on the observed pixels (the left upper part of the target pixel), due to the inductive bias caused by strict adherence to the progressive scan order [7,8]. If the conditional information is located at the end of the autoregressive sequence, it is difficult for the model to obtain the relevant information.

A recent alternative generative model is the Denoising Diffusion Model, which can effectively mitigate the lack of global information [9,10] while achieving comparable or state-of-the-art performance in text [11,12], image [13] and speech generation [14] tasks. Diffusion models are parameterized Markov chains trained to translate simple distributions to more sophisticated target data distributions in a finite set of steps. Typically, the Markov chain begins with an isotropic Gaussian distribution in continuous state space, and the transitions of the chain reverse a diffusion process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to source images. In the inverse process, the current step is based on the global information of the previous step in the chain, which endows the diffusion model with the ability to capture global information.

However, the diffusion model has a non-negligible disadvantage: the time and computational effort involved in generating images are enormous. The main reason is that the reverse process typically contains thousands of steps. Although we do not need to iterate through all the steps during training, all of them are still required to generate a sample, which is much slower than GANs and even autoregressive models.

Some recent works [15,16] have attempted to address these issues by decreasing the number of sampling steps, but the computation cost is still high, as each step of the reverse process generates a full-resolution image.

In this work, we propose the Vector Quantized Discrete Diffusion Model (VQ-DDM), a versatile framework for image generation consisting of a discrete variational autoencoder and a discrete diffusion model. VQ-DDM consists of two stages: (1) learning an abundant and efficient discrete representation of images, and (2) fitting the prior distribution of these latent visual codes via a discrete diffusion model.

By using a discrete scheme, VQ-DDM substantially reduces the computational resources and time required to generate high-resolution images. The common problems of autoregressive models, the lack of global content and the overly large number of parameters, are then solved by fitting a latent variable prior with the discrete diffusion model. Finally, since a bias of the codebook will limit generation quality, while model size also depends on the number of categories, we propose a re-build and fine-tune (ReFiT) strategy to construct a codebook with higher utilization, which also reduces the number of parameters in our model.

In summary, our key contributions include the following:

- VQ-DDM fits the prior over discrete latent codes with a discrete diffusion model. Using a diffusion model allows the generative model to consider global information instead of focusing only on partially seen context, avoiding sequential bias.

- We propose a ReFiT approach to improve the utilisation of latent representations in the visual codebook, which increases the code usage of VQ-GAN from 31.85\% to 97.07\%, while the FID between the reconstruction image and the original training image is reduced from 10.18 to 5.64 on CelebA-HQ 256\times 256.

- VQ-DDM is highly efficient in both number of parameters and generation speed. As shown in Figure 1, using only 120M parameters, it outperforms VQ-VAE-2 with around 10B parameters and is comparable with VQ-GAN with 1B parameters in terms of image quality in image generation tasks. It is also 10 \sim 100 times faster than other diffusion models for image generation [15,10].
